WalkthroughText: An if statement lets your program choose whether to run a block of code based on a boolean condition. Java evaluates the condition in the parentheses to true or false; if it's true, the code inside the if-block runs, and if it's false, that block is skipped and, when present, the else block runs instead. With if/else if/else chains, Java checks each condition top to bottom and runs the first block whose condition is true, skipping all the rest — so exactly one block (or none, if there's no matching else) ever executes. Tracing this kind of code means highlighting each line as it runs and watching each boolean condition "glow" true or false to see which path the program takes.

B" is wrong because the second if's condition is false, so B never prints.
"At least 60" means score >= 60, which includes 60 itself. score > 60 would be false when score is exactly 60, incorrectly printing "Fail".

a > b (4 > 9) is false, so we check a == b (4 == 9), which is also false. Since both are false, control falls to the final else, printing "Z". Only one branch of an if/else if/else chain ever executes.

WalkthroughSteps.Caption: We start with a simple program that declares a temperature variable and will decide what to print based on it.
Line 2 is our first if statement: it checks whether temp is greater than 90.
We substitute temp's value: 85 > 90. That expression evaluates to false, so it glows red.
Since the condition on line 2 is false, we skip its body entirely and jump down to check the else-if condition on line 4.
Substituting again: 85 > 70. This is true, so the condition glows green.
Because this condition is true, control flow enters this branch's body on line 5, and the rest of the chain (any later else) is skipped.
The program prints "Warm" and then jumps past the remaining else block, since only one branch in an if/else-if/else chain ever runs.
